title: Rust version of your millis() wrap check. last is 10 ticks before the wrap, now is 20 after it. What does this print?
explain: wrapping_sub does the same as unsigned C subtraction: the result is modulo 2^32. So 20 - (2^32 - 10) = 30. Plain `-` would panic in a debug build and wrap in release. Use wrapping_sub for tick differences.

title: temp_x10 = -5 (that is -0.5 °C). You print it with / and %. What does this print?
explain: C truncates division toward zero: -5 / 10 = 0. The remainder has the sign of the dividend: -5 % 10 = -5. So you print 0.-5. Print the sign first, then use the absolute value for / and %.

title: Hardware debounce: button with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF. tau = R × C. What does this print (tau in µs)?
explain: R is 10000 Ω, C is 100 nF. R × C_nF = 1,000,000, and divided by 1000 this is 1000 µs = 1 ms. The pin reaches about 63% in one tau and about 99% in 5 tau (5 ms). That is longer than most contact bounce.

title: Button with a 10 kΩ pull-up to 5 V. You press it, so the pin goes to GND. What current flows through the resistor (µA)?
explain: I = U / R = 5 V / 10 kΩ = 0.5 mA = 500 µA. This current flows only while you hold the button. That is why a pull-up is 10 kΩ and not 100 Ω: a small resistor wastes power, a huge one gets noisy.

title: The LED should turn on 2 s after the start. It never turns on. Tap the bug.
explain: start is set again on every pass of loop(), so millis() - start is always about 0. Set start once, at the moment you enter the state (in the transition), not inside the state's own code.

title: main() does GPIOA->ODR |= (1 << 5); An ISR does GPIOA->ODR ^= (1 << 6); Both write other bits of the same register. What can go wrong?
options: The ISR can fire between the read and the write in main(), and its toggle is lost
Nothing, one instruction always writes the register
The compiler refuses to build it
explain: |= is read, modify, write. If the ISR runs after the read, main() writes back the old value of bit 6 and the toggle disappears. Fix: use BSRR (atomic set/reset), or disable interrupts around the update.

title: Ring buffer of 8 bytes (power of two). head starts at 6 and you push 4 bytes. What does this print?
explain: With size N = 8, (head + 1) & (N - 1) wraps without %: 6 → 7 → 0 → 1 → 2. The mask trick works only when N is a power of two.

title: A Pin guard class prints in its constructor and destructor. What does this print?
explain: Objects on the stack are destroyed in reverse order of creation. This is why RAII guards for peripherals unwind cleanly: the last thing you enabled is the first thing you release.

title: A tick counter for an interrupt, written like this. What happens when you build it?
options: It does not compile: using a static mut needs unsafe
It prints done, with a data race warning
explain: Reading or writing a static mut is unsafe, because the compiler cannot stop a data race with an ISR. In embedded Rust use an AtomicU32, or a Mutex<RefCell<_>> from critical-section, and keep unsafe out of the logic.

pr.title: Update head first, saves one variable
pr.author: copilot
pr.body: The UART ISR stores the byte. We move the head update up so we do not need a temp. Buffer size N is 8.

explain: main() reads head to know how many bytes are ready. With the new order head moves before the byte is written, so main() can read a slot that is not filled yet. Also there is no full check, and head and tail should be volatile. Write the data first, publish head last.
